He had known coronary disease. His doctor had him on a statin and blood-pressure medication. He exercised on a bike most days. A new paper cites my N-of-1 as a core feature of next generation longevity science. It explains why my biomarker numbers say less than people think. 

I agree.

Aging is a multi-scale physiological process that we can’t actually measure directly. Biomarkers are like the blind men touching the elephant; able to know a piece, but never the whole.

The processes that dictate aging exist at multiple levels of biological complexity. They interact dynamically at different timescales, across different contexts, and along their own trajectories. 

Aging manifests differently among people, but in highly nuanced and often invisible ways. The static, cross-sectional measures the field is used to can only get us so far.

N-of-1 initiatives like mine can capture some of this nuance, but ultimately fails at generalizability. The authors also critique N-of-1 as able to show "responsiveness but not durability; optimisation but not causality."

The challenge, so far unmet, is modelling the complexity of aging in such a way that the output is not a forecast of biomarkers, but a simulation of aging system dynamics, i.e. one’s health trajectory into the future.

The most intriguing implication of such a model is an improved ability to predict how our decisions will impact us in the future. A choose your own adventure where we can predict the consequences of both our healthy and unhealthy behaviors.

Infrared vs. traditional sauna. Are the benefits really the same?

I get asked this question constantly! My take is that infrared saunas can absolutely produce meaningful heat stress, but they're not necessarily equivalent to traditional Finnish saunas.

Traditional saunas heat the surrounding air, typically around 175-195°F, whereas infrared saunas use radiant heat and generally operate at lower temperatures (110-150°F).

The important question is how much thermal stress you're actually generating.

I personally prefer traditional Finnish saunas. Most of the compelling long-term evidence linking sauna use to lower cardiovascular mortality and dementia risk comes from traditional Finnish sauna studies.

But if infrared is what you have access to, I wouldn't dismiss it!

My recommendation would be to fully preheat the sauna and recognize that you may need a longer exposure to generate comparable heat stress. Importantly, there's no established temperature-duration formula that makes infrared equivalent to traditional sauna.

Infrared saunas can deliver substantial heat stress, but whether they produce the same long-term health benefits as traditional saunas remains an open question.

On the other hand, there is a growing body of evidence that IR saunas, as part of a clinical hyperthermia protocol, can have substantial antidepressant effects in people with major depressive disorder! 

At the end of the day, it seems deliberate heat exposure (up to a point) is broadly beneficial however we get there.
hits.draft_en:
Rhonda Patrick on infrared versus normal saunas. Infrared can give you real heat stress, but it runs cooler, roughly 43 to 65°C against about 80 to 90°C for a traditional Finnish sauna. Most of the strong long-term evidence on heart health and dementia comes from the traditional kind.

Her advice if infrared is what you've got: preheat it properly and expect to stay in a bit longer. Nobody knows yet if the long-term benefits match.

So don't fuss over the type. Use what you can get to, use it regularly, drink water, and talk to your GP first if your heart isn't right.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
Why so many carnivores notice better joints

Cartilage ages mainly through glycation. Collagen in joint cartilage has a half-life measured in decades (estimates up to ~100 years in some tissues). Once formed, the cross-links from advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) stick around. The result is stiffer, less resilient cartilage that doesn’t glide or absorb load the way it used to. Most of those AGEs form endogenously from circulating glucose and reactive dicarbonyls, not from the meat on your plate.

Beef supplies a direct countermeasure: carnosine. This dipeptide is concentrated in muscle and acts as a sacrificial scavenger. It reacts with methylglyoxal and other carbonyls that would otherwise bind lysine and arginine residues on collagen, reducing new AGE cross-links and protein carbonylation. Human data show carnosine supplementation lowers circulating AGE markers and improves glucose handling in people with diabetes. 

Eating the actual muscle delivers the compound in its natural matrix along with the protein and fat that support stable blood sugar.
On a carnivore diet two things happen at once. Endogenous glycation pressure drops because glucose stays lower and more stable, and you continuously supply carnosine that mops up the reactive intermediates that do form. 

That combination plausibly slows the progressive stiffening of cartilage that most people accept as normal aging. It is not magic or a cure for advanced structural damage, but it is a coherent explanation for the repeated reports of less pain, better mobility, and fewer “old joints” once people stop eating the foods that keep glucose elevated all day.
hits.draft_en:
Shawn Baker on why a lot of carnivore eaters say their joints feel better. His argument: cartilage stiffens with age mainly through glycation, where sugar in the blood sticks to collagen and the damage hangs around for decades. Beef carries carnosine, which mops up some of the reactive stuff before it binds.

He's careful to say it's not magic and won't fix advanced damage. It's a plausible explanation for the reports of less pain and better movement.

For blokes with tired knees, the takeaway is simple: keep blood sugar steady, get decent protein, and keep the joints moving. Get the bad ones looked at properly.

Armand Tanny shut the stove off in 1948 and left it off.
He had been on a wrestling tour in Hawaii the year before and had noticed the local men. They were thick, strong, and healthy, and they ate almost everything raw. Fish, meat, shellfish, insects. Tanny came home and started reading Weston Price. The book became the one he trusted. Within a year he had stopped cooking.
He ate roughly three-quarters to a pound and a half of raw meat most days. Beef, liver, tuna. He would wade out from the Santa Monica Pier and kick up clams with his feet, smash them open, and eat the flesh on the spot. Lobster and oysters when he could get them. Nuts, fruit, and some vegetables. No fixed meal plan. He ate when he was hungry.
He was already a capable weightlifter. Within two years of the change he won the 1949 Pro Mr. America and the 1950 Mr. USA. He did it in the years before steroids were common in the sport. He credited the raw meat, particularly the creatine he believed was still intact in it.
He spent the rest of his working life writing for the bodybuilding magazines and running gyms with his brother. He stayed on the raw approach. He died in 2009 at ninety.

The Inuit didn’t get old by eating plants.
Traditional Inuit diet was almost pure animal: seal, whale, fish, caribou, and the fat that came with them. Plant food was seasonal and minimal. Explorers who lived with them in the early 1900s (Stefansson and others) repeatedly noted the absence of the degenerative diseases common in the West at the time—no scurvy, little heart disease, strong teeth into later life, and people remaining active well into their 60s and 70s.
In an era when average life expectancy in Europe and North America was often in the 40s–50s (dragged down by infant mortality, infection, and hard labor), reaching 70+ on a near-zero-carbohydrate, high-fat animal diet was noteworthy. They didn’t have hospitals or modern medicine. They had meat, fat, and a climate that killed the weak early. The ones who made it to old age did so on the same foods their ancestors had eaten for centuries.
Modern contact changed the diet and the health outcomes. The traditional pattern is the one the early observers actually documented.

Why we crave fatty beef: a mammoth-sized clue
Wild aurochs (the ancestors of cattle) were lean, active grazers. Their muscle meat was almost certainly low in intramuscular fat—more like game than a modern steak.
Woolly mammoths were different. Preserved carcasses show thick subcutaneous fat layers (often 8–9 cm on adults) plus concentrated deposits or “humps” around the neck and withers. On a whole-carcass percentage basis, a well-conditioned mammoth was roughly in the same ballpark as a moderately finished modern beef cow (~10–25% body fat seasonally). On an absolute basis it was in another league: hundreds of kilograms of fat on a multi-ton animal.
Ice Age hunters appear to have prioritized that fat. Humans have a practical limit on how much lean protein we can safely metabolize for energy. Large, fat-rich megafauna solved the problem—lean muscle for protein, thick fat for concentrated calories and essential fatty acids. Recent work on Pleistocene hunting preferences points in the same direction: people targeted the biggest, fattest animals and their fattest parts.

That long reliance on fat-rich megafauna may help explain why most people still prefer the fattier cuts of beef. Marbling, ribeye, brisket, and well-finished steaks simply taste better and satisfy more completely than ultra-lean meat. It is not just modern marketing—it may be an ancient preference shaped by the animals that kept our ancestors alive through long winters.
Modern cattle can be finished to similar (or higher) fat percentages, but the ancestral pattern was lean muscle plus abundant external and organ fat. Mammoths delivered both in one massive package.

Why do South Asians get type 2 diabetes at much lower body weights? The answer is in their fat cells.

These are fat cells from two young men with the same BMI. The South Asian man's are on the left. The white man's are on the right.

At the same BMI as white Europeans, South Asians carry more body fat, bigger fat cells, more liver fat, and higher insulin. Here is what the studies show.

In 29 South Asian and 18 white men, average age 27, BMI was 24 vs 23. Body fat was 22% vs 15%. The average belly fat cell was 3,491 vs 1,648 µm² in cross section. Treating the cells as spheres, that is about 3 times the volume of fat per cell on average. The samples in the image show an even larger difference. 3. Fat cell size explains much of the insulin gap.
After adjusting for age, sex and BMI, South Asians had larger fat cells, liver fat of 9.9% vs 2.5%, and higher fasting insulin. Adjusting for fat cell size cut the insulin difference in half.

In 1982 Barry Brenner published a paper in the New England Journal of Medicine.
He proposed that a high-protein diet raised pressure inside the glomerulus, forced the kidney to filter more, and, over time, wore the tissue out. The idea came from animal work in which nephrons had already been reduced. The remaining units overworked. Protein restriction slowed the damage in those models. The paper was widely cited. Protein restriction entered advice for people with kidney disease and, by extension, for anyone who ate a lot of meat.
Later work examined the claim in people whose kidneys were intact. Meta-analyses of trials found that higher protein raised the measured filtration rate, as expected, but did not produce progressive loss of function. Changes in creatinine and other markers of injury did not differ between high- and moderate-protein groups. Observational data in healthy adults likewise failed to show that protein intake predicted later kidney disease. The filtration increase appeared to be an adaptation, not a step toward failure.
The original hypothesis held for kidneys that were already reduced. It did not hold for kidneys that were not. The distinction took decades to settle in the literature. The advice for healthy people did not.

In 1898 the Belgian ship Belgica was trapped in Antarctic pack ice for the winter. The crew lived on tinned meat and other stored rations and began developing scurvy—fatigue, swollen limbs, bleeding gums, and depression. One man died.

The expedition’s American doctor, Frederick Cook, had previously spent time in Greenland and observed that Inuit living almost entirely on fresh game did not get scurvy. He ordered the men to eat fresh penguin and seal meat (often raw or lightly cooked) instead of the preserved stores.
Those who complied improved. 

Ship’s captain Georges Lecointe later described coming out of a near-comatose state after eating a piece of penguin meat and feeling markedly stronger within hours. The crew’s overall condition improved once fresh meat became the main food. 

Those who continued to refuse it fared worse.

Cook’s conclusion was direct: scurvy sat in the gap between tinned food and fresh meat. Cooking and preserving destroyed something essential that raw or lightly prepared fresh meat retained. The Belgica men had no fruits or vegetables available. Their recovery depended on the animals they could kill and eat on the ice.

When humans left hunting and gathering for grain agriculture, the skeletons tell the story. Average height dropped several inches. Dental disease, anemia, and infectious disease rates rose sharply. The new “have-nots”—the early farmers—were shorter, weaker, and sicker than the meat-eating populations they replaced. The ones who kept access to animal foods stayed taller and more robust.
The pattern held for thousands of years. Pastoralists and warriors who ate meat and animal fat consistently outperformed the grain-dependent peasantry in strength and health. Grain was what you ate when meat was scarce or deliberately withheld.
Today the labels have flipped, but the biology has not. Modern elites fund and promote observational studies that downplay meat while elevating grains, seed oils, and ultra-processed carbohydrates as the virtuous choice for everyone else. The same playbook that once kept peasants on bread now uses manipulated science to convince the public that the foods of scarcity are actually optimal.
Meat was never the luxury. Grain was the compromise.

I

The craziest X-ray I’d seen in my entire orthopedic surgery career! 

It’s the spring of 2007 and I’d been on a pretty  intense trauma surgical deployment to Bagram air base in Afghanistan. We had been crazy busy with trauma up to our ears as we were the main referral center for the entire Afghan war theater.  

We treated everyone, US forces, NATO forces, injured civilians to include little kids, Afghan army and even some of the enemy forces that were captured. The trauma itself was unlike anything you’d ever see outside of war. Mangled body parts from high powered explosives were pretty common. 

One evening we received casualties from an IED (roadside bomb) blast. One guy had been injured pretty critically, lost his legs and was unfortunately not going to live. The other guy who was sitting next to him in the truck when they hit the bomb was also injured but would survive. 

This is where it got weird for me.  He was complaining of left leg and foot pain. As was usual we x-rayed everything that hurts ensuring that we got all the joints above and below the area of pain so that we don’t miss any injuries. He knee had definite ligament injuries but no evidence of any knee fracture. 

His foot, on first glance looked like he had a couple of metatarsal fractures, but they had a pretty strange appearance to me. Up to that point in my career I’d seen many thousands of x-rays and this one just wasn’t making sense as to what was really going on. 

Fortunately we had access to a CT scanner, which we often used for complex fractures to figure out best treatment plan. 

We got him in the CT scanner and once we looked at the images, we found out why the x-rays had looked so bizarre. 

He didn’t have any fractures.  What had happened was his buddy who was right next to him in the car was blown up and his foot got blasted apart and was now deeply imbedded into our patients foot, that’s why I couldn’t initially figure it out. 

This type of thing happens from time to time in blast injuries when multiple people are victims. Things  like femoral heads  (the hip ball) get blasted into people’s back and so on. It was the first (and only) time I’d ever seen something like that.  

Fortunately for that guy the surgery to remove a foreign body part from his foot and his knee ligament repairs went very smoothly.  Over 20 years later I’m still amazed by some of the stuff we saw over there!

Can statins impair physiological adaptations to a low-carbohydrate diet? 🤔💊

This question came up in a community chat this morning, so I wanted to address it.

In brief, the answer is possibly.

Not only are statins known to increase insulin resistance and diabetes risk in some people, but some studies have found that statin users exhibit a higher respiratory exchange ratio (RER), consistent with reduced fat oxidation. Other research suggests statins may blunt fat oxidation during exercise. (PMID: 22661624, PMID: 36394519)

That said, a few caveats and practical points.

🧪First, the science.

I'm not aware of any studies directly comparing adaptation to a low-carbohydrate diet in people taking statins versus those not taking statins. And adaptation can be quantified along several dimensions, including fat oxidation, ketone metabolism, and insulin sensitivity.

That would be a fascinating addition to the scientific literature. And frankly, not an especially difficult study to conduct.

🥼Second, the clinical implications.

Let's entertain the possibility that statins impair certain adaptations to carbohydrate restriction, even if the definitive randomized controlled trial is still outstanding.

This could have practical implications for individualized clinical care.

For example, let's assume a patient and physician share the goal of lowering LDL cholesterol and ApoB. In the context of a low-carbohydrate diet, ezetimibe may punch above its weight, potentially because of adaptations in cholesterol absorption and enterohepatic cholesterol handling.

That raises an interesting possibility: Ezetimibe, generally considered a second-line therapy, might offer substantial LDL and ApoB lowering without potentially interfering with the physiological adaptations to carbohydrate restriction.

🎯The broader point:

This isn't about assigning value judgments to medications or personal dietary choices. 

It's about being informed and individualizing care around a person's preferences, lifestyle, and metabolic health.

And that's something we should all be able to get behind.
